grade.first_issue: Step 4 simply asserts, without carrying out the claimed induction, that the infinite intersection is a finite union of sets of multiples. This is the central finiteness/periodicity claim, and the observation that it contains all multiples of its least element does not imply that the whole set is periodic. Thus Rule E applies, capping the score at 3.
grade.summary: The proof correctly reformulates the gcd conditions using prime-factor hitting sets and observes that every sequence term lies in the global accepted set. It also recognizes that a finite union of divisibility classes would yield the desired translation law. However, the essential argument establishing such finiteness is entirely missing and is replaced by an unsupported induction claim and an invalid positive-density-to-periodicity inference. Moreover, the assertion that the sequence is exactly all of C_infinity is false as written because C_infinity may contain accepted integers below a_1; only C_infinity intersected with [a_1,infinity) is enumerated by the sequence.
strengths: Correctly identifies the global set of integers sharing a nontrivial factor with every sequence term.
Correctly proves that every a_n belongs to that global set.
Identifies a viable overall route: prove the global accepted set is a finite union of divisibility classes, then use its period to obtain a fixed index shift.

errors.description: The claim that the increasing sequence is exactly C_infinity does not follow merely from inclusion and increasingness, and is false when C_infinity contains elements below a_1. The correct statement is that the sequence enumerates C_infinity intersected with [a_1,infinity), which also requires a greedy-gap argument.
The claimed induction proving that C_infinity is a finite union of sets mZ is not supplied. This is precisely the difficult central structural step of the problem, rather than a routine omission.
Containing all multiples of the least accepted integer gives positive density but does not imply that the entire set is periodic.
The statement that being a union of arithmetic progressions is equivalent to periodicity is imprecise or false without requiring a finite union of complete residue classes with a common period.
